{"id": "6:81/q03", "question": "What is 'mā ashraktum'?", "turns_on": "Whether mā names the objects, describes an indefinite object, or names the act of association.", "positions": [{"id": "6:81/q03/p1", "position": "It denotes the idols or other powerless objects they associate with God; mā may be a relative pronoun with an understood complement.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi and Ibn ʿAbbas identify idols. Abu Hayyan says mā fits non-rational objects. Ibn ʿAshur supplies the omitted 'with which you associate' from the preceding clause and makes mā the object of ashraktum. Al-Samin and al-Alusi also allow a relative mā with omission."}, {"id": "6:81/q03/p2", "position": "Mā may be an indefinite noun qualified by an omitted description or complement.", "reasons": "Al-Samin and al-Alusi give this syntactic alternative alongside the relative analysis."}, {"id": "6:81/q03/p3", "position": "Mā may be a verbal noun, referring to their act of associating others with God.", "reasons": "Al-Samin gives the paraphrase 'your association'; al-Alusi also lists the verbal noun analysis."}]}
{"id": "6:81/q04", "question": "How is 'you do not fear' joined to Abraham's question?", "turns_on": "Whether wāw coordinates two clauses in the question or introduces a circumstance.", "positions": [{"id": "6:81/q04/p1", "position": "It is coordinated with 'I fear,' so both failures of fear remain within the question and rebuke.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan says the conjunction places both under one rebuke. Al-Samin lists this analysis. Ibn ʿAshur says it condemns both his alleged fear and their actual lack of fear."}, {"id": "6:81/q04/p2", "position": "It is a circumstantial clause: how could he fear while they do not fear the consequences of their shirk?", "reasons": "Al-Samin says an implied subject can precede the present verb negated by lā, while wāw can itself link the circumstance without a resumptive pronoun. Al-Alusi says the circumstance sharpens the contrast between safety and real danger. Ibn ʿAshur prefers this force, comparing 2:44."}]}
{"id": "6:81/q05", "question": "Why does the verse contrast fear of their objects with fear of their association?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:81/q05/p1", "position": "It avoids treating God and idols as comparable objects of fear while exposing their inverted judgment.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan says the changed objects avoid equating God with idols. Al-Samin says Abraham fears their idols whereas they should fear their own act of associating with God. Al-Alusi contrasts their fearless conduct in actual danger with Abraham's safety."}]}
{"id": "6:81/q06", "question": "Why is God named explicitly in the second fear clause?", "turns_on": "Whether the divine name serves emphasis and reverence or a grammatical necessity.", "positions": [{"id": "6:81/q06/p1", "position": "His name magnifies the offense of associating with Him and reflects their failure to honor Him; it was already mentioned in the preceding verse.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports that the first clause omits the name because 6:80 supplied it and to avoid even suggesting Abraham's association with God. He rejects the proposal that the second mention merely provides a pronoun antecedent or marks a different scope of denial; the antecedent was already available and the clauses do not share the proposed negation."}, {"id": "6:81/q06/p2", "position": "The explicit name is needed as the antecedent of the following pronoun, or for a different scope of denial.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports and rejects these explanations: an antecedent was already available, and the two clauses do not combine under one negation."}]}
{"id": "6:81/q07", "question": "What do they fail to fear in 'that you associated with God'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:81/q07/p1", "position": "They fail to fear the danger and consequences of their own association of partners with God.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAshur says min is omitted after 'fear' before an, as often happens; they knew and feared God yet failed to fear their act of association. Ibn Zayd contrasts fearing creatures without fearing God against fearing God alone; Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari stress that God can harm or benefit."}]}
{"id": "6:81/q08", "question": "What does the 'mā' in 'what He did not send down' refer to?", "turns_on": "Whether mā is relative or indefinite; a verbal noun is excluded by sense.", "positions": [{"id": "6:81/q08/p1", "position": "It is a relative noun, the object of 'associate': a partner for which God sent no warrant.", "reasons": "Al-Samin allows a relative noun and rejects the verbal noun here because that would distort the sense."}, {"id": "6:81/q08/p2", "position": "It is an indefinite noun describing a purported partner without divine warrant.", "reasons": "Al-Samin gives this as the other permissible construction."}]}
{"id": "6:81/q09", "question": "How do the prepositions with 'sent down' attach?", "turns_on": "Whether 'upon you' modifies the verb or the noun 'authority'.", "positions": [{"id": "6:81/q09/p1", "position": "Both 'with it' and 'upon you' modify 'sent down'; 'with it' may express accompaniment or cause.", "reasons": "Al-Samin attaches both phrases to 'send down.' {"id": "6:81/q10", "question": "What does sulṭān mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the word denotes evidentiary authority in this verse or its broader sense of power.", "positions": [{"id": "6:81/q10/p1", "position": "It is proof, warrant, or authoritative argument for the alleged partners, which they have not received.", "reasons": "Abu ʿUbayda also offers excuse; al-Zajjaj says clear proof. Ibn Abi Hatim reports Ibn ʿAbbas and seven other authorities saying every Qur'anic sulṭān is proof. Ibn al-Jawzi cites 6:81 and 11:96, 17:33, 30:35, 27:21, 55:33. Ibn ʿAshur says proof prevails over an opponent's mind. Al-Wahidi and al-Jishumi also allow power enabling one to prevail; al-Samin's entry supplies no separate definition."}, {"id": "6:81/q10/p2", "position": "In other Qur'anic contexts sulṭān can mean kingship or coercive power.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi derives it from salāṭa, forceful extension or dominance, on the pattern faʿlān; he cites Satan's denial of power in 14:22 and 34:21. Al-Wahidi and al-Jishumi note the broader sense of enabling power even while discussing this verse."}]}
{"id": "6:81/q11", "question": "What does the lack of revealed authority establish, and could partners ever receive it?", "turns_on": "Whether the denial is solely the lack of disclosed warrant, rules out partnership in principle, or addresses images as a possible prayer direction.", "positions": [{"id": "6:81/q11/p1", "position": "Their claimed partners have no divine warrant; the absence of proof defeats their worship and fear.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari, al-Baydawi and Ibn ʿAshur specify no scripture or command authorizes worship. Abu Hayyan says rational refutation is joined by denial of revealed evidence. Ibn Kathir compares denials of invented religion in 42:21 and 53:23; Study Quran cites 7:33, 7:71, 12:40, 22:71, 53:23. Al-Tabatabai says any genuine partnership would require revelation or outward signs, and neither exists; if a warrant existed fear would be justified. Al-Biqaʿi says none shields them from God's anger. Al-Burhan says the phrase denies any revealed proof for associating the alleged partners."}, {"id": "6:81/q11/p2", "position": "No authorization of genuine divine partners is rationally possible.", "reasons": "Al-Razi presents this implication and compares 23:117. Al-Alusi chooses it, dismissing the Imam's analogy of treating idols as a prayer direction as outside the question of partnership. Al-Tabatabai says the negative wording does not imply God might authorize partners. Al-Burhan adds that the same phrase denies the reality of the alleged partners themselves."}, {"id": "6:81/q11/p3", "position": "The wording denies a revealed command to worship images, while directing prayer toward them is not rationally impossible.", "reasons": "Al-Razi reports this alternative; al-Alusi says the Imam's prayer-direction analogy does not address actual divine partnership."}]}
{"id": "6:81/q12", "question": "What principle about religious claims follows from the missing warrant?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:81/q12/p1", "position": "A religious claim needs evidence from God; an unsupported claim is wrong.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi states the general rule. Al-Bursevi and al-Alusi call the nonexistent 'authority' sarcastic, emphasizing evidence revealed by God. Al-Tabatabai says the absence of evidence itself settles the issue without needing to label the qualification sarcastic or inherent in false partners. {"id": "6:81/q13", "question": "How is 'He sends down' read?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:81/q13/p1", "position": "Both Form II yunazzil and Form IV yunzil are canonical readings.", "reasons": "Qiraat-Er says Form II suggests gradual sending, whereas Form IV suggests a single act."}]}
{"id": "6:81/q14", "question": "How is sulṭān vocalized?", "turns_on": "Whether the lām retains sukūn or assimilates to the preceding ḍamma.", "positions": [{"id": "6:81/q14/p1", "position": "Another reading gives the lām ḍamma.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and al-Samin say it may reflect an independent dialect or vowel following, which would not establish an independent pattern. {"id": "6:81/q16", "question": "Which party deserves security, and on what grounds?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:81/q16/p1", "position": "Those who worship God alone deserve security; idolaters who worship powerless beings without proof do not.", "reasons": "Ibn Jurayj says Abraham's opponents themselves answer that believers in one Lord deserve security. {"id": "6:81/q18", "question": "Why ask 'which of the two parties' rather than 'which of us'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:81/q18/p1", "position": "The indirect phrasing avoids Abraham's self-praise while inviting his opponents to make the judgment.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan and al-Samin stress modesty; al-Samin contrasts a poem that directly asks which of two men is champion. {"id": "6:82/q04", "question": "How is yulbisū read?", "turns_on": "The verb's vocalization and form, and whether Mujahid's wording counts as a reading or an explanatory gloss.", "positions": [{"id": "6:82/q04/p1", "position": "The majority read yalbisū with an open yāʾ, 'they mix'.", "reasons": "Al-Samin gives the majority vocalization and its simple-verb sense."}, {"id": "6:82/q04/p2", "position": "Ikrima reads yulbisū with a rounded yāʾ, 'they make mix'.", "reasons": "Al-Samin derives it from form IV; Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan also report the vocalization."}, {"id": "6:82/q04/p3", "position": "Mujahid's bi-shirk replaces bi-ẓulm as an explanatory wording.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya reports the wording as a reading; Abu Hayyan says it is a gloss, not a canonical reading, since it differs from the written text."}]}
{"id": "6:82/q05", "question": "What does ẓulm mean in this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether context and the Prophetic explanation specify shirk, or the general word and 'mixing' extend the condition to sins or other harms.", "positions": [{"id": "6:82/q05/p1", "position": "It is shirk, associating partners with God, including idol worship.", "reasons": "The recurrent proof is the Prophet's explanation to worried Companions using Luqman 31:13; Tirmidhi grades that report hasan sahih. Abu Bakr, Ibn Abbas, Ubayy, Salman, Hudhayfa, Alqama, Ibrahim, Qatada, Mujahid and others are reported with this gloss. Tabari prefers the sound prophetic report. Ibn Ashur says shirk violates God's exclusive right to worship; Biqai says the indefinite term includes every degree of shirk. Al-Alusi says 'great injustice' points to its fullest instance, though the word can denote other wrongs. Idolaters claimed intercession and nearness to God (39:3). Damghani explicitly illustrates mixing faith with idolatry. Burhan notes that the Ibn Masud report occurs in both Sahih collections."}, {"id": "6:82/q05/p2", "position": "It covers every forbidden act or neglected command, or injury to oneself or others.", "reasons": "Tabari says the fully general reading would assure only the sinless and its proponents restrict the verse's audience; others leave lesser sinners to God's will. Mawardi records general and restricted versions. Baydawi mentions 'sin'. A commentator cited by Tabatabai includes religious and worldly harm, but Tabatabai rejects treating accidental bodily damage as the verse's concern and says that scope would leave no real instance. Ibn al-Jawzi's root definitions include putting something outside its place or acting concerning what one does not own; Tabarsi cites poetry on cutting a camel wrongly and diverting rain. Ibn al-Jawzi also records ordinary injustice (2:35 and other verses), the proverb ma zalam, undug land, claims of oppression, a severe oppressor, not leaving a path, and tooth-water or shine. Tabatabai traces expansion from social injustice to lawbreaking, sin and accidental harm."}, {"id": "6:82/q05/p3", "position": "It includes grave sins that corrupt the effect or reward of faith, but excludes minor wrongs expiated by obedience or repentance.", "reasons": "Al-Jubba'i and al-Balkhi say grave sins cancel reward. {"id": "6:82/q06", "question": "How is the verse's clause structure parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether the opening relative phrase is an answer or independent subject, how the nested nouns predicate one another, and whether the two wāw clauses are relative, circumstantial or independent.", "positions": [{"id": "6:82/q06/p1", "position": "The relative phrase is a subject; 'those' starts a nested subject clause, with 'for them is security' as its predicate.", "reasons": "Nahhas makes alladhina and ulaika successive subjects, al-amn the subject of lahum, and the full nested clause the first predicate; al-Alusi prefers this broad parse. Al-Samin gives the explicit three-subject nesting; Ibn Atiyya makes al-amn nominative and lahum prepositional predicate. Abu Hayyan notes an omitted subject or predicate can be supplied."}, {"id": "6:82/q06/p2", "position": "The relative phrase is predicate of an omitted 'they'; 'those' begins a new sentence.", "reasons": "Al-Samin ties this to a spoken answer by Abraham, his people, or God instructing the Prophet, and permits an omitted 'say/they said'. Al-Alusi calls the omitted-subject analysis remote."}, {"id": "6:82/q06/p3", "position": "'Those' is apposition to the relative phrase and 'for them' its predicate, with security a governed subject or delayed subject.", "reasons": "Al-Samin records both variants of the placement/function of lahum and al-amn; al-Alusi calls the appositional alternative remote."}, {"id": "6:82/q06/p4", "position": "'Those' is a second subject, 'for them' its predicate, and 'security' an active subject.", "reasons": "Al-Samin lists this as a fourth independent-report parse."}, {"id": "6:82/q06/p5", "position": "'Those' is a separator; 'for them is security' predicates the relative phrase.", "reasons": "Attributed to Nahhas and al-Hawfi by al-Samin, who calls it odd because demonstratives do not serve as separators; Abu Hayyan calls their analysis remote."}, {"id": "6:82/q06/p6", "position": "'They did not mix' continues the relative clause.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and al-Samin allow coordination under alladhina."}, {"id": "6:82/q06/p7", "position": "'They did not mix' is a circumstantial clause.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and al-Samin cite 19:20 as a parallel negative circumstance. Al-Samin rejects Ibn Asfur's rarity claim and Ibn Khuruf's mandatory-waw claim."}, {"id": "6:82/q06/p8", "position": "'And they are guided' is a second nominal sentence, either independent or circumstantial.", "reasons": "Nahhas gives it a subject-predicate structure. Al-Samin allows independence or circumstance; Ibn Ashur prefers the full sentence as coordinated with the earlier nominal sentence, citing 64:1 and 57:2."}]}
{"id": "6:82/q07", "question": "What security is promised?", "turns_on": "Whether security excludes any punishment or only eternal punishment, and whether it includes worldly and inward safety.", "positions": [{"id": "6:82/q07/p1", "position": "Safety from God's punishment, especially on Judgment Day.", "reasons": "Tabari contrasts believers' safety with idolaters' worldly fear and painful afterlife punishment. Ibn Abbas specifies punishment; Jishumi Judgment Day; Tabarsi adds reward; Bursawi says only shirk-free believers have this protection. Ibn Kathir includes the Day of Judgment. The believer who dies without shirk ultimately escapes the Fire, says Wahidi. Burhan links the Prophet's saying that sincere testimony bars one from Hell to the believers' security, and infers from 37:35 that the disbelievers' refusal to say it led to their entry into Hell."}, {"id": "6:82/q07/p2", "position": "Safety specifically from eternal punishment; lesser sinners remain between fear and hope.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports this qualification and says even a sinless-condition reading does not prove all sinners certainly punished. The commentator quoted by Tabatabai includes religious punishment and worldly consequences, with mercy or punishment possible in both."}, {"id": "6:82/q07/p4", "position": "It is true inward safety from turning to any refuge besides God.", "reasons": "Ibn Tahir says the believer relies on God in trials; Qashani makes freedom from hidden self-association its condition. Tabatabai elsewhere cites assurances of God's friends having no fear or grief."}, {"id": "6:82/q07/p5", "position": "Absolute safety from punishment is unavailable to ordinary accountable people.", "reasons": "A commentator cited by Tabatabai reserves it for the awe of spiritually complete people; Tabatabai objects that this would leave the verse without a real instance or argumentative force."}]}
{"id": "6:82/q08", "question": "What does it mean that they are guided?", "turns_on": "Whether guidance names truth and religion now, entrance to Paradise, or both worldly and final guidance.", "positions": [{"id": "6:82/q08/p1", "position": "They follow truth and God's religion.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas says directed to God's religion; Tabarsi says judged to follow truth; Bursawi and Al-Alusi contrast them with all others in error. {"id": "6:82/q09", "question": "What emphasis does the wording give to security and guidance?", "turns_on": "Whether the pronoun in 'they are guided' functions as a separator or the subject of a second sentence.", "positions": [{"id": "6:82/q09/p1", "position": "The demonstrative and nominal clauses strongly establish the promised predicates for the described believers.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says 'those' points to their description as the basis of entitlement, comparing 2:5; the lam marks exclusive settled possession, stronger than merely 'they are safe'. Tabatabai notes several linked nominal clauses."}, {"id": "6:82/q09/p2", "position": "If 'they' is a separator, guidance is exclusive to the monotheists described.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur cites 2:55 and 9:104 for the construction."}, {"id": "6:82/q09/p3", "position": "If 'they are guided' is its own nominal sentence, it adds guidance without grammatical exclusivity.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says this makes coordination smoother, with analogies at 64:1 and 57:2."}]}
{"id": "6:82/q10", "question": "Who speaks the answer to Abraham's question?", "turns_on": "Whether this clause is quoted speech continuing the exchange or God's independent verdict, and whether the idolaters could credibly concede Abraham's case.", "positions": [{"id": "6:82/q10/p1", "position": "God declares the ruling that resolves Abraham's dispute.", "reasons": "Tabari prefers this: idolaters would not concede the monotheism they opposed. {"id": "6:82/q14", "question": "What follows for believers who commit major sins?", "turns_on": "Whether faith can coexist with grave sin, whether 'wrongdoing' means shirk or sin generally, and whether lack of assurance entails certain punishment.", "positions": [{"id": "6:82/q14/p1", "position": "A believer may sin gravely; absence of shirk assures eventual escape from the Fire, while lesser punishment remains possible.", "reasons": "Wahidi explicitly infers ultimate security for one dying without shirk. {"id": "6:82/q15", "question": "How does this answer complete Abraham's argument?", "turns_on": "Whether the connection is read as the immediate adjudication of 6:81 alone or as part of the sura's wider prophetic argument.", "positions": [{"id": "6:82/q15/p1", "position": "It decides which side of the dispute deserves security: exclusive worship of God defeats idols and their claimed protection.", "reasons": "Tabari links it to 6:81. {"id": "6:82/q16", "question": "What authority does the transmitted explanation carry?", "turns_on": "The evidentiary rank of Prophetic and Companion explanations against arguments drawn from general wording and theology.", "positions": [{"id": "6:82/q16/p1", "position": "The Prophetic explanation specifying shirk is decisive for this verse.", "reasons": "Tabari prefers Ibn Masud's sound report; Abu Hayyan rejects Zamakhshari's grave-sin reading because the Prophet expressly explained the word. Burhan presents Bukhari's report as a Prophetic gloss, alongside Prophetic glosses of easy reckoning as presentation (84:8), strength as archery rather than cavalry (8:60), and worship as supplication (40:60). Burhan identifies the report explaining wrongdoing as shirk as present in both Sahih collections; Ibn Ashur invokes the Prophet's clarification to identify the intended injustice."}, {"id": "6:82/q16/p2", "position": "A solitary report cannot override a categorical argument for the sin reading.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports the Mu'tazili response to the hadith; their argument is that shirk and faith are opposites and 'mixing' must therefore refer to sin."}, {"id": "6:82/q16/p3", "position": "Companion exegesis has transmitted authority, though the basis and strength of reports require assessment.", "reasons": "Al-Hakim likens Companion interpretation to a raised report. Abu al-Khattab questions its binding force; Burhan favors evidentiary force because tafsir is transmitted, while explaining Ahmad's warning that many reports lack sound connected chains, not that none are sound. Ibn Masud's knowledge of revelations and learning ten verses with practice illustrate the tradition. The discussion of 9:14 raises an analogy about human action and divine power."}, {"id": "6:82/q16/p4", "position": "An interpretation may specify the intended application of general wording.", "reasons": "Itqan says Ibn Abbas recognized the broad wording while naming its intended referent, just as Companions heard general ẓulm and the Prophet specified shirk. Tabatabai treats varied applications of wrongdoing as degrees of a general word."}]}
{"id": "6:82/q17", "question": "Does Abraham's community need only monotheism because an existing civil code supplied law?", "turns_on": "The proposed chronology, the code's polytheism, and whether later Torah material can establish Mosaic borrowing.", "positions": [{"id": "6:82/q17/p1", "position": "Yes; a commentator proposes Hammurabi's code supplied civil and ethical rules.", "reasons": "The proposal explains a monotheism-only condition for Abraham's people while Muslims have a complete revealed law."}, {"id": "6:82/q17/p2", "position": "No; the Hammurabi proposal fails historically and textually.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says its chronology does not fit Abraham, Hammurabi invokes many gods, and the Torah's legal material cannot show Mosaic dependence on Hammurabi: the Torah was lost in Babylonian captivity and later reconstructed amid Babylonian customs; nonrevealed rules can still be sound."}]}
{"id": "6:82/q18", "question": "What relative revelation order is inferred from the Prophetic explanation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:82/q18/p1", "position": "Al-An'am followed Luqman.", "reasons": "Tabatabai identifies the 'righteous servant' quoted in the report as Luqman and infers the order from the explanation's use of Luqman 31:13."}]}
{"id": "6:82/q19", "question": "How is the nearby statement about raising degrees read?", "turns_on": "The person marker and case/construction of 'degrees', with a separate parallel at 12:76.", "positions": [{"id": "6:82/q19/p1", "position": "It is read with nūn and a genitive annexation.", "reasons": "Jishumi lists this as one reading of the adjacent 'We raise' wording."}, {"id": "6:82/q19/p2", "position": "It is read with nūn and an accusative indefinite 'degrees'.", "reasons": "Jishumi lists this as another reading."}, {"id": "6:82/q19/p3", "position": "At the parallel passage in Yusuf, Yaqub reads a yāʾ form.", "reasons": "Jishumi distinguishes this variant at 12:76 from the local readings."}]}
{"id": "68:17/q01", "question": "Who is meant by 'We tested them'?", "turns_on": "Whether the plural is confined to the historical deniers or includes their type.", "positions": [{"id": "68:17/q01/p1", "position": "The Meccan or Quraysh deniers addressed in the preceding passage.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Ṭabarī and many later authors identify the addressees as Meccans; Ibn ʿĀshūr links the pronoun to the preceding deniers (68:8, 14–15). {"id": "68:17/q03", "question": "What does balāʾ mean here, and how can God test?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:17/q03/p1", "position": "A trial or affliction that exposes conduct; divine testing assigns duties without giving God new knowledge.", "reasons": "Jishumī says trial, testing and examination are synonymous and that acts become manifest although God knew them beforehand, so the expression is figurative of His treatment. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ notes ibtilāʾ in Last Day descriptions and surveys the agents of fitna: God, Satan, magic, hypocrites, disbelievers, and people testing each other. She endorses al-Rāghib's and Ibn al-Athīr's observation that balāʾ and fitna more commonly signal hardship, while acknowledging trials through prosperity and adversity together. {"id": "68:17/q07", "question": "Is 'the garden' a particular known orchard or a generic parable?", "turns_on": "Whether the definite article points to a known place or serves the parable generically.", "positions": [{"id": "68:17/q07/p1", "position": "A particular orchard known from accounts about Yemen and its owners.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī says the story was locally known; Ibn ʿĀshūr associates it with Darwan; Elmalılı says Arabs knew it.
